claims.text: Conventional automotive exhaust catalysts use aggregated PGM nanoparticles, such as Pt on CeO2 or related supports.
A high-entropy spinel oxide containing 5–7 cations can be synthesized for use as a catalyst support.
The high-entropy spinel support will promote strong metal–support interactions.
The high-entropy spinel support will stabilize isolated or very finely dispersed PGM atoms.
The proposed performance comparison will be conducted at 300–600 °C in a lean oxidizing atmosphere with repeated thermal cycling.
A high-entropy spinel can form a homogeneous lattice with a uniform elemental distribution.
The high-entropy oxide lattice provides abundant oxygen vacancies.
The homogeneous high-entropy lattice strongly anchors isolated PGM atoms.
PGM anchoring by the high-entropy oxide minimizes PGM sintering and dissolution.
Oxygen vacancies and configurational disorder in the support modify the local electronic structure of PGM active sites.
The modified PGM electronic environment enhances binding and activation of oxygenated species used in exhaust conversion.
Configurational disorder improves resistance to high-temperature sintering of the PGM.
The high-entropy-supported PGM catalyst will have a lower light-off temperature than a conventional supported, aggregated-PGM catalyst.
The high-entropy-supported PGM catalyst will provide higher oxidation conversion efficiency than the conventional catalyst.
The high-entropy-supported PGM catalyst will retain activity better during thermal cycling than the conventional catalyst.
Effective exhaust-pollutant conversion can be maintained while using less PGM.
Phase segregation or insufficient PGM dispersion would limit the proposed benefits.
Conditions beyond the stability window of the high-entropy oxide may degrade catalyst performance.
High-entropy multimetallic systems have shown improved activity and durability in electrocatalysis.
The magnitude of activity and durability gains under realistic automotive exhaust conditions is not yet quantitatively known.
